E0858.summary: An unnamed poet, called “the initiated poet”, whose Metamorphoses Atwood cites for an apt figure of the celestial elements.
E0858.body: Atwood cites the initiated poet's *Metamorphoses* as offering an apt figure of the same celestial elements she is discussing: “the arising circulation of Mature from the four concentering winds” [III.2 ¶36]. The text names him only by this description.

forms: the initiated, who celebrated her Mysteries in the Eleusian fane
E0859.summary: The initiated who celebrated the goddess's Mysteries in the Eleusian fane, cited by Atwood for how they described the multinominal goddess.
E0859.body: Atwood invokes the initiated who celebrated the goddess's Mysteries in the Eleusian fane to illustrate the multinominal goddess as they described her [III.3 ¶62].

E0860.summary: Nature's principle of perfection, held shut up by the bond of coagulation.
E0860.body: Atwood speaks of Nature's “Inner Light and principle of perfection” [III.2 ¶61], identifying the Inner Light with her principle of perfection, which is shut up by the bond of coagulation.

E0861.summary: The hidden meaning of the alchemical records, kept apart from their literal sense.
E0861.body: Atwood states: “In almost all the records of Alchemy, the inner sense is held aloof from the literal” [III.4 ¶16] — the records' inner meaning is kept apart from what they say on the surface.

E0862.summary: In a quoted Hermetic passage, the innermost chamber of life, where the Argent vive is prepared and coagulated.
E0862.body: In a footnote quoting Hermes with a Scholiast's comment, the Argent vive is said to be prepared in the innermost chamber: “It is prepared in the innermost chamber of life, and there it is coagulated” [I.3 n9]. The place is glossed as the ‘ultimate axle of each created life’ [I.3 n9]. The voice is the quoted authorities, not Atwood directly.

E0863.summary: The trained seeker or operator of the Art, who must learn what, where and how to obey, inquire, will and hope.
E0863.body: Atwood refers to “all the care that is taken to train the true Inquisitor” [III.1 ¶38]: the seeker of the Art must be trained in what, where and how to obey, inquire, will and hope.

E0864.summary: In the later Table Talk, the enclosing of the lower life, figured by the Walls of Troy and done in a great resonance.
E0864.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer begun 1860), Atwood reads the Walls of Troy as a figure “of the insphering of the lower life; it is done in a great resonance” [APP ¶49] — apparently the enclosing or bounding of the lower life within a sphere.

E0865.summary: The one unclean thing that enters the Stone, moving the gold to putrefy; evil at first but necessary, it finally gives the work its force and perfection.
E0865.body:
Atwood says nothing unclean enters the Stone “except One thing, which is the Instrument moving the gold to putrefy” [III.1 ¶61]; “it is the very grave of the rational light” [III.1 ¶61]. It is evil at first but necessary, and once returned through the natural Alembic it constitutes the force and perfection of the work [III.1 ¶61].

Identities: “it is called by them Typhon, Satan, Aquafoetida, Ignis Gehanna, Mortis Immundities, etc.” [III.1 ¶61].

E0866.summary: The alliance and power man enters by conditioning himself in obedience to the Divine Will.
E0866.body: Atwood writes that by conditionating in obedience to the Divine Will “he comes into the integral alliance and power” [IV.4 ¶23].

E0867.summary: In ordinary use the power of demonstrative knowing; in its highest sense the purified divine sight that beholds God, separates contraries, and is identified with the true man and the intelligible.
E0867.body:
**Two senses.** Atwood distinguishes Intellect in ordinary use — the power by which we know and prove things demonstratively — from its highest sense: a sight “called Intellect, which is capable of beholding God” [II.1 ¶38]. In that sense “True Intellect, he says, is that which is essentially the most essential of that which is most essential” [II.1 ¶37]; mortals lack it through generation. Identities: “the true man, according to Plato and Aristotelians, is this Intellect” [II.1 ¶35]; “that Intellect is the same with the intelligible” [II.1 ¶37].

**Quoted authorities.** Plotinus asks of the gods' beauty, “What else, however, is it but Intellect through which they are such?” [II.4 ¶29]. Atwood, endorsing Synesius and Anaxagoras, makes Intellect the superior separating power: “Intellect above all things separates whatever is contrary to the true purity of phantastic Spirit” [III.1 ¶20], purifying and attenuating that Spirit and extending it to Divinity; and “Intellect is infinite and possesses absolute power, and is not mingled with any thing; but is alone by itself.” [III.1 ¶22]. Its special part is apparently the sequestatrix, though this reading is uncertain.

**In the method.** Drawing on Aristotle and Plotinus: “That Intellect must be assumed which is most perfectly purified” [III.1 ¶23]; it gives the soul a sudden Light, and “this Light is from Intellect, and is also It” [III.1 ¶23]. Without its light it suffers “the wanderings and anguish of Intellect so artificially isolated on the plain of Truth” [III.1 ¶28]. It is “the watchful eye of Intellect, well advised and able” that cuts off the sleeping Will [III.1 ¶68]. The Poemander testimony shows “the operative revelation of Intellect” [III.3 ¶59], known by experience.

**Fable readings.** “that court of King Alcinous, to which Ulysses became admitted, is the dominion of Intellect” [IV.1 ¶22], also signified by the Phoeacian ships. The fable conceals “the principiating action of Intellect but the methodical art of the same subtle Antecedent” [IV.2 ¶7] — its bringing itself into natural effect by begetting a supernatural offspring.

E0868.summary: Aristotle's name, as reported, for human reason: subordinate to essential intellect and perfected only by a new awakening.
E0868.body: Atwood reports that Aristotle “denominates human reason, intellect in capacity” [II.1 ¶34]. It is subordinate to essential intellect and reaches its perfection only by a new awakening.

E0869.summary: The Intellect from which, Atwood says, the Greeks derived nature mediately, fixing her true Being in the Law of Universals.
E0869.body: Atwood says the Greeks “derived nature mediately from a certain Intellect in energy, but without distinction, fixing her true Being in the Law of Universals” [III.2 ¶34].

E0870.summary: Intellectual activity in Elysium, whose permanence alone is accompanied by eternity and in which the exemplary Image of Universal Nature is revealed.
E0870.body: Atwood writes that “eternity is consubsistent only with the permanence of intellection itself” and that “this is the Intellection in Elysium where the exemplary Image of the Universal Nature also is revealed” [II.4 ¶15].

E0871.summary: Illumination proceeding from the Divinity within when the conditions are duly offered; Reason is its temple.
E0871.body: Atwood speaks of the “Intellectual Ilumination which proceeds, when the conditions are duly offered, from the Divinity within” [III.1 ¶5], and calls Reason its temple. The book's spelling is “Ilumination”.

E0872.summary: Plato's term, as given, for the sudden kindling of a self-nourishing light in the soul; Schelling describes waking from it as from death.
E0872.body: Atwood applies the term to Plato's account of a self-nourishing light suddenly kindled in the soul after long converse and a conforming life, “speaking in like manner of the Intellectual Intuition” [II.3 ¶50]. She also quotes Schelling: “We awaken from the Intellectual Intuition, says Schelling, as from a state of death” [IV.2 ¶33] — waking into created personality, where He can no longer be known.

E0873.summary: The self-evident law of reason (intuition, Universals) that proves and orders ordinary inquiry; abstract to the moderns, nature's efficient force to the ancients.
E0873.body: Atwood presents the Intellectual Law as the self-evident law of reason — intuition, Universals — that proves and orders ordinary inquiry. Moderns recognise “that same Law which the former recognizes but as an abstract boundary of thought only, having its object in sensibles” [II.1 ¶35], whereas the ancients treated it as the subject of nature's efficient force. A higher principle (Intellect/Wisdom) “bears the same relation to our Intellectual Law as does this to the reasoning faculty” [II.1 ¶39].

E0874.summary: The heroic, separable, thrice-refined purpose personified by many heroes and by Hermes' ‘our Son’, which passes through darkness, death and the Stygian waters.
E0874.body:
Atwood speaks of “that heroic, separable, triply refined intellectual purpose” [III.1 ¶36], personified by many heroes and passing through darkness, death and the Stygian waters.

Identities [III.1 ¶36]: “This is that prolific Mustard-seed, and Light of divine Faith”; it is “our Son, as Hermes calls him, born a king”; and “Such was the Caduceus of Hermes --- the Golden Bough, the ferrying Cup of Hercules”.

E0875.summary: The field whose upper grades are aspired to through labours and dangers.
E0875.body: Atwood mentions “those who aspire to the upper grades of Intellectual Science” [II.2 ¶14], who do so through labours and dangers.

E0876.summary: In Proclus as quoted, direct intellectual sight: contact with the Intelligible and union with the Demiurgic Intellect, opposed to syllogistic science.
E0876.body: Quoting Proclus, Atwood sets Intellectual Vision against syllogistic science: “But it is that which subsists according to Intellectual Vision itself: a contact with the Intelligible, and a union with the Demiurgic Intellect.” [II.4 ¶41]

E0877.summary: In Proclus as quoted, what the soul becomes when assimilated as far as possible to the whole intelligible universe.
E0877.body: Proclus, quoted, speaks of “the soul thus becoming an Intellectual World” [II.4 ¶41] when it is assimilated as far as possible to the whole intelligible universe.

E0878.summary: In a Zohar passage quoted by Atwood, the name Thought takes on becoming Spirit; Life springs forth by Intelligence excruciated.
E0878.body: In the Rabbi's account from the Zohar, Thought on becoming Spirit takes this name: “Arrived at this estate, it takes the name of Intelligence” [III.3 ¶78]. In the next paragraph Life springs forth “as by Intelligence excruciated” [III.3 ¶79].

E0879.summary: The object of intellectual contact, existing beyond the mind; the higher of the twofold nature, in which it is better for the soul to abide.
E0879.body:
Quoted authorities speak here. The Divine Oracle makes the Intelligible the object of intellectual contact, understood with the Flower of the mind but never wholly comprehended: “That thou mayest learn the Intelligible, for it exists beyond the mind.” [II.4 ¶48]. The Platonic Successor speaks of “having transcended the Intelligible” [II.4 ¶41] toward the Ineffable.

Plotinus and Porphyry, quoted: “And since there is a twofold nature, one intelligible and the other sensible, it is better indeed for the soul to abide in the intelligible world” [III.2 ¶50]; one is assimilated to it by being established in one's own essence.

E0880.summary: Empedocles' twofold natural procedure, as Atwood reports it: the sensible derived as an image from the intelligible as its exemplar.
E0880.body: Atwood reports Empedocles' twofold procedure of nature, “deriving the latter as an image from the former as an exemplar” [III.2 ¶38] — the sensible as image of the intelligible.

E0881.summary: The ordered progression, called gods by the Greeks, through which the perfected souls of the Initiated pass before contemplating the Highest Unity.
E0881.body: Atwood describes the perfected souls of the Initiated passing through “the whole progression of Intelligible Causes, by the Greeks called gods” [II.4 ¶39] before contemplating the Highest Unity.

E0882.summary: An inner agent which, awakened by too great excitation, could cause a disseveration in the Chaos.
E0882.body: Atwood warns of excess: “lest by too great excitation the internal agent awakening should cause a disseveration in the Chaos” [IV.1 ¶15].

E0883.summary: The adepts' inner fire, essential to the Hermetic work, which alone, purified, perfects it, unlike external or natural fires.
E0883.body: Atwood names “that internal fire and vessel of the adepts, so essential to the accomplishment of the Hermetic work” [II.1 ¶6]. She contrasts it with the external coal fire and the fire of the natural life, which only alter: “the internal alone is able, being purified, to perfect the work begun” [III.1 ¶43].

E0884.summary: The light within the matter, made manifest as the Dragon is occultated, which once manifest must enter another life and die again.
E0884.body: Atwood describes the light within the matter becoming manifest as the Dragon is occultated; once manifest to sense, it must enter another life and die again [I.3 n43, n44]. Related expressions appear nearby — ‘metallic light’, ‘fermenting light’ and the vital light: “The vital light, as we have before explained, is centrally hidden in nature until it is drawn forth” [I.3 n46] — but the text does not explicitly assert they are the same.

E0886.summary: Psellus's term, as cited, for the initiate's inward seeing of the Divine Light without form or figure, distinguished from the Superinspection.
E0886.body: Atwood cites Psellus for the initiate's inward seeing of the Divine Light without form or figure: “This is the Introspection which Psellus speaks of, as distinguished from the Superinspection which takes place in Hades” [II.3 ¶46].

E0887.summary: Inward testing, without which inbred evil cannot truly be discovered.
E0887.body: Atwood holds that inbred evil cannot be truly discovered without inward testing: “or even discover it truly without introspective proof” [IV.4 ¶17].

E0888.summary: A complete process that must be passed through before the work is perfected; not further defined.
E0888.body: Atwood states that “it is not perfected unless the whole introversion is passed through” [III.1 ¶21]. The text here does not define the process further.
